consensus_summary: The sword primarily symbolizes the Word of God as a penetrating spiritual weapon of truth, conviction, and judgment (Eph 6:17; Heb 4:12; sword from Christ’s mouth in Revelation), with common alternatives of divine judgment/wrath, civil authority, gospel-induced division, violence, and (lesser) martyrdom or sorrow.
book_summary: The sword symbolizes war and the word of judgment, illustrated by the great sword that takes peace from the earth and the flaming sword that guards the way.
consensus_core_identification: the Word of God (as spiritual weapon)
book_core_identification: war and the word of judgment
boundary_disagreement: Consensus treats Word of God as the default/primary symbolic sense (with judgment often merging only in the mouth-sword texts) and war/judgment as secondary or context-specific; the book elevates war plus word-of-judgment (via the Rev 6:4 great sword and Gen 3:24 flaming sword) as the identification itself.
material_contradiction: The consensus primary identification (Word of God) and the book’s identification (war and the word of judgment) cannot both serve as the core symbolic referent in the same sense; accepting the book replaces the dominant Christian teaching rather than merely narrowing its cases.
rationale: All consensus responses converge on the Word of God as the settled primary meaning in Christian teaching, grounded in explicit NT equations and the Christological mouth-sword, while listing judgment and war only as common alternatives. The book’s entry instead names war and the word of judgment, illustrated solely by the red-horse great sword (people killing one another) and Eden’s flaming sword. Although “word of judgment” overlaps the Revelation sense that sometimes merges with the Word of God, the book’s pairing with war and its choice of non-Word citations replace rather than refine the central referent; the cores therefore contradict.
strongest_objection: Explicit equations of the sword with the word of God (Eph 6:17; Heb 4:12) and the consistent reading of the sword from Christ’s mouth make Word of God the primary sense; the book’s citations support only secondary war/judgment imagery and omit those texts.
